title: HashSet internals — backed by HashMap, dummy PRESENT value

s1_definition.profdef: HashSet is literally a **wrapper around HashMap**. Internally: `private transient HashMap<E, Object> map`. Every element you add becomes a KEY in the HashMap. The VALUE for every key is the same dummy constant: `private static final Object PRESENT = new Object()`. `add(e)` calls `map.put(e, PRESENT)` — returns true if the key was new (put returned null), false if already existed. `contains(e)` calls `map.containsKey(e)`. `remove(e)` calls `map.remove(e)`. ALL HashSet behavior — O(1) add/contains/remove, no duplicates, unordered — comes directly from HashMap. Hashing, buckets, load factor 0.75, treeification at 8 — all inherited from HashMap.
s1_definition.analogy: HashSet is a HashMap in disguise. Imagine a filing cabinet (HashMap) where every drawer has a label (key = your element) and inside every drawer is the SAME rubber stamp saying "PRESENT" (dummy value). You only care about the drawer LABELS (the set elements), not what's inside. Adding a duplicate label? HashMap says "this key already exists" → HashSet says "element already in set — rejected."
s1_definition.oneliner: HashSet = HashMap where elements are KEYS and values are a dummy `PRESENT` object. All behavior (O(1), hashing, buckets, treeify) inherited from HashMap.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** HashSet is literally a **wrapper around HashMap**. Internally: `private transient HashMap<E, Object> map`. Every element you add becomes a KEY in the HashMap. The VALUE for every key is the same dummy constant: `private static final Object PRESENT = new Object()`. `add(e)` calls `map.put(e, PRESENT)` — returns true if the key was new (put returned null), false if already existed. `contains(e)` calls `map.containsKey(e)`. `remove(e)` calls `map.remove(e)`. ALL HashSet behavior — O(1) add/contains/remove, no duplicates, unordered — comes directly from HashMap. Hashing, buckets, load factor 0.75, treeification at 8 — all inherited from HashMap.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** HashSet is a HashMap in disguise. Imagine a filing cabinet (HashMap) where every drawer has a label (key = your element) and inside every drawer is the SAME rubber stamp saying "PRESENT" (dummy value). You only care about the drawer LABELS (the set elements), not what's inside. Adding a duplicate label? HashMap says "this key already exists" → HashSet says "element already in set — rejected."

**One line to remember:** HashSet = HashMap where elements are KEYS and values are a dummy `PRESENT` object. All behavior (O(1), hashing, buckets, treeify) inherited from HashMap.

sections.s3_banking: **Problem — The trade deduplication service needed to track unique trade IDs.** Developer used ArrayList + contains() — O(n) per check, 10K trades = 10K × 10K = 100M comparisons. Fix: HashSet — O(1) per contains(), 10K trades = 10K lookups. From 30 seconds to 50 milliseconds.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is a set of account IDs added to a `HashSet`, which is internally backed by a `HashMap`.

**Step 1.** `add("SAV2001")` is translated into `map.put("SAV2001", PRESENT)`, where PRESENT is a shared dummy value object.

**Step 2.** The HashMap computes the hash of the ID and stores it as a key in the right bucket, so duplicate adds of Rajesh's ID map to the same key and are ignored.

**Step 3.** A membership check `contains("SAV2001")` simply calls `map.containsKey`, giving O(1) average lookup since the set is really just the key side of a HashMap.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ HashSet = HashMap WRAPPER ═══

  HashSet.add("SAV2001")
    → HashMap.put("SAV2001", PRESENT)
       → hash("SAV2001") → bucket index → store Node(SAV2001, PRESENT)

  HashSet.add("SAV2001")  ← duplicate!
    → HashMap.put("SAV2001", PRESENT)
       → finds existing key → returns old PRESENT → add() returns false!

  HashSet.contains("SAV2001")
    → HashMap.containsKey("SAV2001")
       → hash → bucket → walk chain → equals() → true!

  ═══ INTERNAL VIEW ═══
  HashMap inside HashSet:
  bucket[3]: Node(hash, "SAV2001", PRESENT, null)
  bucket[7]: Node(hash, "CUR3001", PRESENT, null)
  bucket[12]: Node(hash, "FD4001", PRESENT, null)
  Every value is the SAME PRESENT object!

  ═══ SET VARIANTS ═══
  HashSet      → backed by HashMap     (unordered, O(1))
  LinkedHashSet→ backed by LinkedHashMap (insertion order, O(1))
  TreeSet      → backed by TreeMap      (sorted, O(log n))
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
HashSet is literally a HashMap wrapper. Internally it has `HashMap<E, Object> map` and a static dummy `PRESENT = new Object()`. `add(e)` calls `map.put(e, PRESENT)` — returns true if new, false if duplicate. `contains(e)` calls `map.containsKey(e)`. All HashSet properties come from HashMap: O(1) average operations, default capacity 16, load factor 0.75, treeification at 8 collisions, allows one null element. Elements MUST implement proper `hashCode()` and `equals()` because they're used as HashMap keys.

Same pattern: LinkedHashSet wraps LinkedHashMap (maintains insertion order), TreeSet wraps TreeMap (maintains sorted order). In banking: trade deduplication — HashSet.contains() is O(1) vs ArrayList.contains() O(n). For 50K trades: HashSet takes 5ms, ArrayList takes minutes. Always use Set for uniqueness checks, never List.contains() for large collections.
